content: 1. It is crucial to monitor the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) among people living with HIV, particularly those with a baseline CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm³. This is because a low CD4 count indicates advanced immunosuppression, which requires prompt intervention to reduce morbidity and mortality. 2. The numerator for this indicator is the number of people living with HIV who started ART during the reporting period and had a baseline CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm³. The denominator is the total number of people living with HIV who initiated ART during the same reporting period, regardless of their baseline CD4 count. 3. Data collection for this indicator relies on HIV patient monitoring tools, such as patient records, electronic medical records (EMRs), ART registers, and laboratory records. The recommended reporting period is 12 months. 4. Late ART initiation is a core indicator that highlights the importance of timely treatment initiation to prevent disease progression and improve outcomes. This indicator also includes disaggregation by gender, age, and key populations, such as men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. 5. Viral load (VL) testing is a critical component of HIV care. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends routine VL testing at six months and 12 months after ART initiation, and annually thereafter. This ensures that virologic suppression is achieved and maintained, which is essential for the 95-95-95 targets. 6. The numerator for VL testing coverage is the number of people living with HIV on ART for at least six months who had at least one routine VL test result during the reporting period. The denominator is the total number of people living with HIV on ART for at least six months. 7. Early viral load testing, particularly at six months after ART initiation, is vital for identifying individuals who may require adherence counseling or regimen adjustments. The time window for early VL monitoring includes a margin of ± one month, allowing tests to be conducted between five and seven months after ART initiation. 8. Virologic suppression is a key measure of ART effectiveness. The numerator for this indicator is the number of people living with HIV on ART who achieved virologic suppression (VL < 1000 copies/mL) at six months after ART initiation. The denominator is the total number of people eligible for VL monitoring at six months. 9. Monitoring ART-related toxicities is essential, as prolonged exposure to antiretroviral drugs can lead to adverse reactions. These toxicities are a common reason for treatment discontinuation, non-adherence, or drug substitution. The numerator is the number of ART patients who stopped treatment or switched regimens due to toxicity during the reporting period, while the denominator is the total number of ART patients during the same period. 10. Early infant diagnosis (EID) of HIV is critical for initiating ART in children with confirmed HIV infection. The numerator is the number of HIV-exposed infants who received a virological HIV test within two months of birth, while the denominator is the estimated number of HIV-positive women who delivered during the reporting period. 11. ARV prophylaxis for HIV-exposed infants is a key strategy to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV. The numerator is the number of HIV-exposed infants started on ARV prophylaxis at birth, and the denominator is the number of HIV-positive women who delivered in a facility within the past 12 months. 12. Providing ART to HIV-positive pregnant women during pregnancy and delivery is essential for preventing vertical transmission. The numerator is the number of HIV-positive pregnant women who received ART during pregnancy and/or at labor and delivery. The denominator can be program-based (women attending antenatal care or delivering in a facility) or population-based (all HIV-positive pregnant women who delivered during the reporting period). 13. Viral suppression at labor and delivery among HIV-positive pregnant women is a critical service quality measure. The numerator is the number of HIV-positive pregnant women on ART who were virally suppressed (<1000 copies/mL) at delivery. The denominator can be program-based (women delivering in a facility with a VL test) or population-based (all estimated HIV-positive pregnant women). 14. Disaggregation of data by gender, age, key populations, and timing of ART initiation (e.g., during pregnancy or labor) is essential for understanding gaps in care and tailoring interventions to specific groups. This ensures that HIV programs are inclusive and address the needs of diverse populations.
